title: With Due Respect (Vol. 2) -- Ch. 9: Regaining Public Trust
keywords: one consideration... should be the limit
Internal Rules of the Supreme Court
primary_topics: Chapter 9 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 2) -- CJP's September 5, 2010 Inquirer column, written as judiciary retirees discussed how to 'revive or regain public esteem' for a Supreme Court whose 'residual credibility' had been battered by recent controversies

His rejection of a proposal to 'stop criticizing and just heedlessly defend the Court' -- arguing that effective defense must be 'objective, truthful, and credible,' since 'false hosannas' and 'undeserved praise is disguised ridicule'

His unsparing account of the Court's own 'fodder for critics' -- chiefly the 'dismaying flip-flop' in League of Cities v. Comelec (a 2008-2010 series of reversals on the Cityhood Laws) and justices writing 'No part' or 'In the result' with no explanation, in violation of the Internal Rules

His prescription: that justices be 'more prudent, more precise, and more decisive,' since 'transparency, accountability, and integrity' -- not PR hype or 'blind faith to defend the indefensible' -- are the Court's 'best antidotes' to public distrust
sub_topics: The retirees' project: judiciary retirees mulling how to 'help revive or regain public esteem' for the Court, recognizing that while criticism and dissent are healthy, 'the whole Court must enjoy residual credibility at all times' -- distinguishing 'the shifting winds of public emotion' from 'long-term trust'

The stakes (impossible and inevitable): the Court must keep its role as 'the last bulwark of democracy,' lest 'our very nationhood would be splintered'; paraphrasing JFK, 'if peaceful resolution of disputes becomes impossible, violent revolution would be inevitable'

The rejected shortcut: a proposal to 'stop criticizing and just heedlessly defend the Court' was 'quickly shot down' as 'unacceptable, impractical, and illogical' -- to defend effectively one must be 'objective, truthful, and credible,' for 'false hosannas would skew the institution's integrity' and 'undeserved praise is disguised ridicule'

The Court as its own worst critic's source: between Marites Vitug's 'Shadow of Doubt' and the 'bludgeoning' of the decision letting GMA appoint the new CJ, the Court and its justices kept 'providing fodder for critics'

The League of Cities flip-flop chronology: Nov. 18, 2008 (6-5, Carpio ponente) struck down the Cityhood Laws; March 31, 2009 denied the first MR and barred further pleadings; April 28, 2009 (6-6) denied a second MR; Dec. 21, 2009 (6-4, Velasco ponente) flipped to uphold them; Aug. 24, 2010 (7-6, Carpio ponente) flopped back to unconstitutional

Why the flip-flop alarms: a 'change in the composition of the Court' might explain it, but 'some incumbents also changed sides'; citing retired Justice Vicente Mendoza that the US Supreme Court never reconsiders (reconsideration being disallowed), CJP suggests 'one consideration... should be the limit,' since vote-switching 'with nary an explanation' invites suspicion of inadequate study or 'succumbing to pressures'

Individual fodder: even after the Internal Rules took effect, some justices wrote 'No part' or 'In the result' beside their signatures 'without any explanation,' in 'stark violation of the Rules' and the Constitution -- lapses CJP pressed his former colleagues to justify

The prescription: justices should be 'more prudent, more precise, and more decisive'; 'transparency, accountability, and integrity' are the 'best antidotes to media's slamming,' whereas 'misleading public relations hype or blind faith to defend the indefensible would only ricochet and intensify distrust'

notable_anecdotes: The retirees' huddle: CJP frames the column as a conversation among judiciary retirees 'mulling how we could help revive or regain public esteem for the Supreme Court we all love.'

Shooting down the cheerleaders: he recounts a colleague proposing they simply 'stop criticizing and just heedlessly defend the Court,' a suggestion 'quickly shot down' as 'unacceptable, impractical, and illogical.'

The five-step flip-flop: he reconstructs the League of Cities saga blow by blow -- unconstitutional (Nov. 2008), MRs denied (2009), then constitutional (Dec. 2009), then unconstitutional again (Aug. 2010) -- as 'incredible' institutional fodder.

Mendoza on the US Court: he invokes retired Justice Vicente Mendoza's point that the US Supreme Court 'has never reconsidered any of its decisions, simply because reconsideration is not allowed,' to argue for a one-reconsideration limit.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 9 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 2), CJP's September 5, 2010 Inquirer column, grows out of a conversation among judiciary retirees 'mulling how we could help revive or regain public esteem for the Supreme Court we all love.' While criticism and dissent are healthy, he argues, 'the whole Court must enjoy residual credibility at all times,' distinguishing 'the shifting winds of public emotion' from 'long-term trust' -- and the stakes are high, for if the Court loses its place as 'the last bulwark of democracy,' then, paraphrasing JFK, 'if peaceful resolution of disputes becomes impossible, violent revolution would be inevitable.' He rejects a colleague's proposal to 'stop criticizing and just heedlessly defend the Court' as 'unacceptable, impractical, and illogical': to defend effectively one must be 'objective, truthful, and credible,' since 'false hosannas would skew the institution's integrity' and 'undeserved praise is disguised ridicule.' Much of the damage, he says, is self-inflicted -- from Marites Vitug's 'Shadow of Doubt' and the 'bludgeoning' of the decision letting GMA appoint the new chief justice, to the 'dismaying flip-flop' in League of Cities v. Comelec, which he reconstructs step by step: unconstitutional in November 2008 (6-5, Carpio), motions denied through 2009, constitutional in December 2009 (6-4, Velasco), then unconstitutional again in August 2010 (7-6, Carpio). A change in the Court's composition might explain it, but 'some incumbents also changed sides,' and -- citing retired Justice Mendoza that the US Court never reconsiders -- he urges that 'one consideration... should be the limit,' because switching votes 'with nary an explanation' invites suspicion of inadequate study or 'succumbing to pressures.' He likewise faults justices who still write 'No part' or 'In the result' without explanation, in 'stark violation of the Rules.' His remedy: justices must be 'more prudent, more precise, and more decisive,' for 'transparency, accountability, and integrity' -- not PR hype or 'blind faith to defend the indefensible' -- are the Court's 'best antidotes' to distrust.
